paras.text: The Standard Fire Policy, M C L Five Hundred Point Two Eight Three Three, Audio Lecture

Welcome to the standard fire policy chapter, the backbone statute of Michigan property insurance. Every fire policy sold in this state, and every homeowners policy built on top of a fire chassis, has to contain a specific list of provisions, and that list lives in one section: M C L five hundred point two eight three three. Know this statute cold and you can point to the exact letter of the exact subsection that controls most Michigan property claim arguments.

This statute sits in Chapter twenty eight of the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, the chapter called Fire Insurance Contracts, running from section two eight zero four to section two eight six six. Section two eight three three itself was added in nineteen ninety, by Public Act three oh five, with immediate effect on December fourteenth of that year. It replaced an older approach. Until the end of nineteen ninety one, Michigan had a separate section, five hundred point two eight three two, that spelled out an actual standard fire policy form. The same nineteen ninety act repealed it, effective January first, nineteen ninety two. Today the legislature's website shows only a one-line compiler's note saying it, quote, pertained to form of standard policy, end quote. So here is an honest gap: I cannot tell you word for word what that old form said, because its text was not verified against a primary source. What is certain is that the modern statute, in subsection two, still leans on that repealed section as a floor: every fire policy must contain, at minimum, the coverage that was in the standard fire policy under former section two eight three two. The old form is gone as a document, but its substance survives as an incorporated minimum.

Now let's walk the current statute. Subsection one is a list, lettered a through s, of provisions every fire policy issued or delivered in Michigan must contain. This is the state's non-negotiable checklist, no matter which company writes the policy.

Letter a is the actual cash value floor. The policy has to cover, at minimum, the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss. A carrier can offer more, replacement cost coverage, for example, but it can never offer less than actual cash value as the baseline.

Letter b is the core peril and the removal rule. Minimum coverage is direct loss by fire and lightning, and on top of that, pro rata coverage for five days for property that gets moved to another location to save it from a covered peril. Picture furniture carried out of a burning house, sitting in the yard for a few days and getting rained on: this five-day removal provision is what protects it.

Letter c lets the policy be void for misrepresentation, fraud, or concealment. Letter d requires the policy to state what property is not covered, and letter e requires it to state what perils are not covered. Letter f requires a statement of what conditions suspend or restrict coverage, and letter g requires a provision for waiving or changing a policy term.

Letter h covers the insured's right to cancel. The insured can cancel at any time, and the insurer's minimum earned premium is not less than the pro rata premium for the expired time, or twenty five dollars, whichever is greater. So if someone cancels early in the term and the pro rata number works out to eight or nine dollars, the insurer still keeps twenty five. Letter i is the mirror image: the insurer's right to cancel. The insurer can cancel at any time too, but it has to mail written notice to each named insured, at their last known address, at least ten days before cancellation takes effect, postage fully prepaid. The same twenty five dollar or pro rata minimum earned premium applies, and if there's excess premium the insurer isn't tendering up front, the cancellation notice itself has to say that excess will be refunded on demand.

Letter j is the mortgagee clause, and it matters because almost every damaged house has a mortgage. If loss is payable to a mortgagee who isn't named as an insured, the insurer can cancel that mortgagee's interest by giving the mortgagee at least ten days' written notice. The piece people forget: if the insured never gets around to filing proof of loss, the mortgagee itself, once notified, has sixty days to render its own proof of loss. And if the insurer pays the mortgagee while denying the underlying claim against the homeowner, the insurer steps into the mortgagee's shoes for recovery, what we call subrogation, up to the amount it paid, without cutting off the mortgagee's own right to sue. Alternatively the insurer can pay off the mortgage debt entirely and take an assignment of the debt and mortgage. Either side, or both together, can sue to recover their respective shares.

Letter k is the pro rata other-insurance rule: if a second policy also covers the same peril, the first insurer's liability is capped at its pro rata share, not the whole loss. Letter l simply requires the policy to state its notification requirements when a loss occurs.

Now we get to the appraisal clause, letter m, probably the single most tested provision in this whole section. If the insured and the insurer can't agree on the actual cash value or the amount of the loss, either party can make a written demand for appraisal. Once that demand goes out, each side has twenty days to pick its own competent, independent appraiser and name that appraiser to the other side. The two appraisers then have to agree on an umpire. If they can't agree within fifteen days, either side can ask a circuit court judge, in the county where the loss happened or where the property sits, to pick the umpire for them. The appraisers set the amount item by item. If they agree, that's the number. If they don't, they kick their disagreement to the umpire, and a written agreement signed by any two of the three, meaning the two appraisers, or one appraiser plus the umpire, sets the final amount of loss. Each party pays for its own appraiser; the umpire's fee and other appraisal expenses split fifty-fifty. Memorize the numbers here: twenty days to name an appraiser, fifteen days to agree on an umpire, any two of three sign off. And memorize the limit of what appraisal actually does. The statute's own words limit it to the amount of the loss or the actual cash value. Whether something is covered at all is a coverage question, and the Court of Appeals held in Maksym versus Auto Owners, a published twenty twenty six decision, that an insured is not entitled to appraisal on items whose coverage is still in dispute. That dispute goes to court, not to the appraisal panel. The appraisal chapter covers the cases.

Letter n gives the insurer options besides paying cash: it can repair, replace, rebuild, or simply take the damaged property. Letter o shuts the door on abandonment: there is no right for the insured to just hand over the wreckage and expect a full payout as though it were a total loss without going through the claim process.

Letter p is the payment clock: the loss is payable within thirty days after the insurer receives proof of the amount of loss. But notice the opening words: except as otherwise provided in section two eight four five. Section two eight four five is Michigan's municipal escrow-withholding statute, and where it applies, part of the payment can be legitimately delayed and redirected under its own separate rules. So a payment that runs past thirty days because of a two eight four five escrow is not a violation of the thirty day rule.

Letter q is the suit-limitation clause, and it has a built-in trap. An action under the policy must be commenced within one year after the loss, or within whatever longer period the policy itself specifies. But here's the twist: that clock is tolled, meaning paused, from the moment the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability. So an insured does not always have exactly one year from the date of loss to sue. If the insured notifies the carrier promptly and the carrier takes a year and a half to formally deny the claim, the suit clock has been sitting paused that entire time, and only starts ticking again once that formal denial happens. Letter r requires the standard subrogation provision: the insurer steps into the insured's shoes to recover from any other party responsible for the loss. And letter s sets the effective time for every fire policy under this section: twelve zero one a m, standard time, at the location of the property.

Subsection two, as I mentioned, ties the whole thing back to that repealed former section two eight three two, requiring the minimum coverage of that old standard fire policy as a floor, on top of everything in subsection one.

Now let's talk about the escrow-withholding statutes, because these two sections, five hundred point two eight four five and five hundred point two two two seven, are constantly confused with each other. Both let a municipality require an insurer to withhold twenty five percent of a fire-loss settlement, as security to make sure a damaged structure actually gets fixed or torn down instead of left standing as a hazard. But they apply to different population bands. Section two eight four five covers the smaller municipalities: cities, villages, and townships in counties under four hundred twenty five thousand people, as long as that particular city, village, or township doesn't itself have fifty thousand or more residents. Its residential cap has been twelve thousand dollars since two thousand fifteen, adjusted every January first by the consumer price index. Section two two two seven is the mirror statute for the bigger jurisdictions: counties of four hundred twenty five thousand or more, plus any city, village, or township of fifty thousand or more even inside a smaller county. And two two two seven also covers a wider range of perils, not just fire and explosion, but vandalism, malicious mischief, wind, hail, riot, and civil commotion.

Here's the critical twenty twenty four update. Public Act eighty two of twenty twenty four amended section two two two seven, and only two two two seven, raising its residential cap from twelve thousand dollars to twenty four thousand dollars, effective July first, twenty twenty four, and switching its adjustment date to every July first instead of January first. Section two eight four five was not touched. It's still on the old twelve thousand dollar, January first schedule. The two statutes now run on different numbers and different calendars.

Which brings us to the current bulletin. DIFS Bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S, issued and entered June second, twenty twenty six, and signed by Director Anita G Fox, sets the section two two two seven maximum withholding amount at twenty five thousand ninety dollars, effective July first, twenty twenty six, through June thirtieth, twenty twenty seven. This bulletin supersedes the prior year's bulletin. And for context, the year before that, July first twenty twenty five through June thirtieth twenty twenty six, the figure was twenty four thousand ninety six dollars. Twenty five thousand ninety dollars, and it belongs to section two two two seven, not two eight four five.

Both escrow statutes share the same internal rhythm. The municipality gets fifteen days after the withholding notice to say it wants the money escrowed, or the funds default to the insured. Once escrowed, the insured has ten days to object. If a mortgage is in default, the treasurer releases funds to the first mortgagee within ten days of a written request. If nobody shows reasonable proof of repair or demolition within one hundred twenty days, the municipality can use the retained money itself to secure, repair, or demolish the structure, returning any leftover to the insured. An insured who wants to sue a municipality to get withheld proceeds back has three years from the original withholding notice. There's also an opt-out: file a qualifying repair contract with the insurer within fifteen days of the final settlement, consent to paying the contractor directly, and have the insurer notify the municipality, and there's no withholding at all.

Let's connect this to how an actual homeowners policy is worded. A modern H O three policy is built on the same fire coverage base this statute governs, and its Section One Conditions roughly track two eight three three's subdivisions. A condition called Appraisal mirrors letter m's twenty day and fifteen day mechanics. Our Option mirrors letter n's repair, replace, rebuild, or take language. The Mortgage Clause mirrors letter j. And Suit Against Us mirrors letter q, with one careful point: some policies give two years to sue, and in Michigan that longer period controls, because letter q says one year or the policy's period, whichever is longer. The statute is a floor, not a ceiling. A policy may lengthen the suit window; it can never shorten it below one year or drop the tolling.

Finally, let's ground this in what a restoration contractor actually experiences on a job. Letter j's mortgagee mechanics matter because loss checks are so often made out jointly to the homeowner and the bank, and a slow homeowner can trigger that separate sixty day mortgagee clock. Letter m's appraisal right belongs to the insured, not the contractor. A contractor whose detailed estimate supports the homeowner's own appraisal demand is doing legitimate work; a contractor who personally demands appraisal or negotiates the umpire for a fee is edging into unlicensed public adjusting under a different statute, five hundred point one two two two. Letter n's insurer-option clause is why a "we're sending our own crew" letter from a carrier is a right the statute actually gives them, even if rarely used. Letter p's thirty day payment clock is the number a contractor plans draws and cash flow against. And letter q's one year, tolled suit clock matters because a contractor's timeline and lien strategy have to be planned against the homeowner's outer legal deadline.

Let's recap the numbers before we go. Twenty five dollars or pro rata, whichever is greater, for either party's cancellation. Ten days' mailed notice for an insurer cancellation, and ten days' notice to cancel a mortgagee's interest, with sixty days for a mortgagee to render its own proof of loss. Twenty days to name an appraiser, fifteen days to agree on an umpire, any two of three sign the amount. Thirty days to pay after proof of amount of loss, subject to section two eight four five. One year to sue, or the policy's longer period, tolled from notice to formal denial. Twelve zero one a m as the effective time. Twenty five percent withholding under both two eight four five and two two two seven, but two eight four five's cap is twelve thousand dollars on a January schedule, while two two two seven's cap is twenty four thousand dollars on a July schedule since Public Act eighty two of twenty twenty four, now twenty five thousand ninety dollars for July twenty twenty six through June twenty twenty seven under Bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S. Lock these numbers in.
